1:1.text: And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

provenance.other: “nurture and admonition” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:4. The Book of Mormon reproduces the whole prepositional phrase, article and all.
provenance.significance: Enos opens a book about a son by borrowing the New Testament's one sentence addressed to fathers. Recover Ephesians 6:4 and the borrowed clause is the positive half of a prohibition — 'provoke not your children to wrath: BUT bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord' — and wrath is the word the chapter will hand to the Lamanites at 1:14, who 'swore in their wrath'. The father who did not provoke his son to wrath stands at the head of a chapter whose antagonists are defined by it.

1:1.note: 'He taught me in his language, and also in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.' Six words carried over intact from the only KJV verse that contains them, and carried over into their original setting: a father's duty to a son. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion, but the phrase is a KJV singleton and the situation matches, which is as good as short borrowings get. It also sets the chapter's first source: Enos 1:1-4 works down Ephesians 6 in order — 6:4 here, 6:12 at 1:2, 6:18 at 1:4.

1:1.text: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.

provenance.other: “knowing that he was a just man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 6:20. “a just man” on its own occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, so it is the participle, not the epithet, that carries the identification.
provenance.alternative: 'A just man' is a stock KJV epithet (Noah, Joseph, Cornelius, Lot); the agreement may be the accident of a common phrase meeting a common participle.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of the uncomfortable kind. The KJV's one sentence about knowing that someone is a just man is Herod's about John the Baptist — a regard that ends in a beheading — and the verse closes 'he heard him gladly', which is what Enos 1:3 says of his father's words. Enos takes the syntax of a man who listened to a prophet and killed him anyway, and turns it into the syntax of a son who listened and was converted. Whether the writer heard the Herod resonance is unknowable; the catalogue's business is to record that the sentence-shape is Mark's and nobody else's.

1:1.note: 'Knowing my father, that he was a just man.' Insert two words into Mark 6:20 and you have Enos 1:1 exactly. ADJUDICATING.md §4 warns that Herod verses score high and mean nothing — 'exceeding glad' outranked everything in 1 Nephi 3 — so this one is proposed with that warning in view; what distinguishes it is that the shared run is a singleton and reaches six words, not two.

1:2.text: For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.

provenance.other: “wrestle” — this exact base form, not “wrestled” or “wrestlings” — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:12. The Jacob-cycle verses (Genesis 30:8, 32:24, 32:25) all use an inflected form of the same root and are the narrative source; Ephesians 6:12 alone gives the word Enos actually uses, and it alone names a spiritual rather than a physical struggle.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's key. Enos calls his prayer 'the wrestle which I had BEFORE God' — and Ephesians 6:12, the one KJV verse that uses the word of a spiritual contest, defines the Christian's wrestle by what it is NOT against: 'we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities.' Recover that context and Enos's preposition is doing work: the wrestle is neither against flesh (as his ancestor Jacob's was, Genesis 32) nor against the powers, but before God himself. And it stands eight verses after 1:1's source and six before 1:4's, in the same chapter of the same epistle, read straight through.

1:2.note: 'I will tell you of the wrestle which I had before God, before that I received a remission of my sins.' The noun is doing all the work, and in the KJV it has exactly two homes: Jacob at Peniel and Paul at Ephesus. Enos, the son of a Jacob, takes both — the narrative from Genesis 32 (see the companion link) and the vocabulary of religious struggle from Ephesians 6:12. Note that 1830 reads 'before that I received', a KJV-style expletive 'that' which 1920 deleted; the first edition is fractionally more biblical than the current text here, as at 1:8 and 1:11.

1:2.text: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.

provenance.other: The wrestling narrative occupies Genesis 32:24-25; Genesis 32:30 supplies the face-to-face conclusion that Enos 1:27 answers. There is no reproduced clause here — the link is at the level of narrative form, which is why kjvSpecific is 'no'.
provenance.significance: The son of Jacob describes a solitary night-long wrestle before God from which he emerges blessed and forgiven. Genesis 32 supplies every structural element: alone (32:24), all night 'until the breaking of the day', a refusal to let go 'except thou bless me' (32:26), a new name, and the conclusion 'I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved' (32:30). Enos 1:2-5 keeps the sequence and answers it point for point — the night (1:4), the blessing ('thou shalt be blessed', 1:5), and, twenty-two verses later, the face: 'then shall I see his face with pleasure' (1:27). The typology is not decorative. Enos's father is named Jacob, so the son is re-running his father's namesake's night, and the record he wrestles for at 1:13-16 is the record of the covenant that Peniel established.

1:2.note: 'The wrestle which I had before God.' The word alone would be an Ephesians link; the shape of the whole episode is Genesis 32's. A man alone, a contest lasting into the night, a demand that is not released until it is granted, and a face-to-face ending. What Enos changes is the adversary: Jacob wrestled with a man and prevailed, Enos wrestles before God and is forgiven. Given that Enos's father is Jacob (Jacob 7:27), the chapter is a son deliberately taking up his father's name-story and converting a contest into a prayer.

1:3.text: Let these sayings sink down into your ears: for the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men.

provenance.other: “sink down into your ears” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 9:44. Enos keeps the verb and the depth adverb and substitutes the heart for the ears.
provenance.alternative: The metaphor of words sinking is not rare in English devotional prose of the 1820s, and the shared vocabulary is one verb.
provenance.significance: Luke 9:44 is a father's words about a son — 'the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men' — that the disciples were given to keep and did not understand ('they understood not this saying', 9:45). Enos reverses the failure: his father's words about eternal life did sink, and deep. The sinking-into metaphor is Luke's; the organ is changed from ears to heart, which is Proverbs 4:21's ('keep them in the midst of thine heart'), the passage Enos will reach for again at 1:12.

1:3.note: 'The words which I had often heard my father speak, concerning eternal life, and the joy of the saints, and the words of my father, sunk deep into my heart.' The KJV has one verse for words sinking, and it is Jesus telling disciples to let a saying about his death sink down. Enos's clause is the same instruction fulfilled rather than issued. Note that 1830 repeats 'and the words of my father' — a doubling 1920 deleted as dittography, but which reads as the Hebraic resumptive the rest of the chapter is written in.

1:3.text: All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, yea, all ye beasts in the forest.

provenance.other: “beasts in the forest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 56:9. The KJV's usual formula is 'beasts of the forest' (Psalm 50:10, 104:20, Isaiah 56:9's neighbours); the preposition Enos uses is the rarer one.
provenance.alternative: A man hunting in a forest may simply be described in the ordinary way, and 'in' rather than 'of' may be idiom rather than borrowing.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 56:9 summons the beasts of the forest to devour, and the reason follows immediately: 'his watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark' (56:10). Enos goes out to hunt those beasts and comes back a watchman — the chapter ends with him 'prophesying of things to come' (1:19) and preaching 'exceeding harshness' (1:23) to keep a people from destruction, which is precisely the duty Isaiah's watchmen abandoned. If the echo is real, the hunting trip is the last thing Enos does as one of the beasts' hunters and the first as Israel's watchman.

1:3.note: 'I went to hunt beasts in the forest.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and the preposition is the unusual one, which is what raises this above coincidence. The catalogue records it at moderate confidence because the sense is unrelated — Isaiah is issuing a summons to judgment, Enos is reporting a hunt — and because the interest lies entirely in what Isaiah 56:9's context does to Enos's vocation, not in the sentence itself.

1:4.text: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker.

provenance.other: “our maker” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 95:6, and “kneel before the LORD our maker” likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse. No other KJV verse joins kneeling to God as maker.
provenance.significance: Hardy's one cross-reference for this book lands on the verse that starts the chapter's second sustained source. Psalm 95 is not merely a kneeling verse: it is the psalm the Book of Mormon then follows in order. 95:6 kneels before the maker (Enos 1:4); 95:7 says 'To day if ye will hear his voice' and Enos 1:5 immediately produces a voice; 95:11 swears that the unbelieving shall not enter 'into my rest', and Enos's soul rests at 1:17 and goes to 'the place of my rest' at 1:27. Three stops in the psalm's own order across a chapter of twenty-seven verses, exactly as Ephesians 6 is worked at 1:1-4.

1:4.note: 'I kneeled down before my Maker.' The one KJV verse that puts a worshipper on his knees before God under the title 'maker' is Psalm 95:6, and Enos has the posture, the preposition and the title. What follows in the psalm follows in the chapter: the voice of 95:7 arrives at Enos 1:5, and the rest of 95:11 arrives at 1:17 and 1:27. The 1830 capital in 'my Maker' is the compositor's, not evidence, but the title itself is.

1:4.text: Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;

provenance.other: “prayer and supplication” occurs in exactly six KJV verses (1 Kings 8:38, 1 Kings 8:54, Daniel 9:3, Acts 1:14, Ephesians 6:18, Philippians 4:6), so the phrase alone identifies nothing. What identifies Ephesians 6:18 is its position: eight verses after 1:2's source and fourteen after 1:1's. 1 Kings 8:54 is the only one of the six that also has kneeling ('kneeling on his knees'), and stands behind the posture Psalm 95:6 supplies.
provenance.alternative: 'Prayer and supplication' is a KJV formula available from six verses and from the whole of English liturgical usage; taken alone this would be common vocabulary.
provenance.significance: The third and last stop on the Ephesians 6 run. 6:4 gave 1:1 its father, 6:12 gave 1:2 its wrestle, and 6:18 — 'praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance' — gives 1:4 its unremitting day-and-night petition. Ephesians 6:18 is the closing instruction of the armour passage, the sentence that tells the reader what the wrestle of 6:12 is actually conducted with; Enos 1:2 named the wrestle and 1:4 supplies the weapon, in Paul's order.

1:4.note: 'I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication, for mine own soul; and all the day long did I cry unto him.' The phrase is not rare, and this link rests on sequence rather than rarity: three consecutive Enos verses draw on Ephesians 6:4, 6:12 and 6:18 in that order, which is the same behaviour 1 Nephi 2-4 shows toward Hebrews 11. Ephesians 6:18's 'praying always' and 'watching thereunto with all perseverance' are what Enos's day-long and night-long crying enacts.

1:5.text: And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee.

provenance.other: “thy sins are forgiven thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 5:20. The parallel healings read 'thy sins be forgiven thee' (Matthew 9:2) and 'thy sins are forgiven' (Luke 7:48); the Book of Mormon has Luke 5:20's form precisely.
provenance.significance: The words are Jesus's to the paralytic let down through the roof, and Luke's point in that scene is the scribes' objection: 'Who can forgive sins, but God alone?' (5:21). Enos hears the sentence from a disembodied voice with no mediator present, which is the scribes' question answered by construction — the speaker must be God. Note too that Luke 5:20 grants forgiveness 'when he saw their faith', and faith is the ground the voice gives at Enos 1:8 ('because of thy faith in Christ').

1:5.note: 'Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee, and thou shalt be blessed.' Five words reproduced exactly from the single KJV verse that contains them, with only the vocative changed from 'Man' to 'Enos'. Short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and catalogued as a quotation anyway on the strength of the singleton, on CONVENTIONS §2's principle. The second clause, 'thou shalt be blessed', closes the Genesis 32 frame opened at 1:2: Jacob would not release his adversary 'except thou bless me', and the voice grants Enos what Jacob had to extort.

1:5.text: And it was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entering in of the cave. And, behold, there came a voice unto him, and said, What doest thou here, Elijah?

provenance.other: “there came a voice unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 19:13. The New Testament voices come 'from heaven' (Matthew 3:17, Mark 9:7, Acts 11:9) or 'to him' (Acts 10:13); only 1 Kings 19:13 has the construction Enos uses.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one instance of a voice coming to a person is the sequel to the still small voice at Horeb, and it comes to a prophet who has spent the chapter asking to die and has just been fed and let sleep. Recover it and Enos's scene acquires Elijah's grammar: a solitary place, a night, a wordless exhaustion, and then a voice that begins by naming the man — 'What doest thou here, Elijah?' / 'Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee.' Elijah's naming is an accusation and Enos's is an absolution, which is the whole difference between the two chapters.

1:5.note: 'And there came a voice unto me saying, Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee.' The clause is built in two halves out of two different KJV singletons — the voice from 1 Kings 19:13 and the absolution from Luke 5:20 — and neither half occurs anywhere else in the Bible. That is the chapter's method in miniature: an Old Testament frame filled with New Testament speech, which is also what 1:2 does with the wrestle.

1:6.text: In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began;

provenance.other: “cannot lie” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Titus 1:2. Hebrews 6:18 has 'it was impossible for God to lie' and Numbers 23:19 'God is not a man, that he should lie'; neither has the modal Enos uses.
provenance.significance: One two-verse sentence in Titus supplies four separate points of this chapter, and in Titus's order: 'in hope of ETERNAL LIFE' (Enos 1:3, his father's subject), 'which God, that CANNOT LIE, promised before the world began' (1:6), 'but hath in DUE TIMES manifested his word' (1:16, 'in his own due time'), 'through PREACHING, which is committed unto me' (1:26, 'I must preach and prophesy'). This is a third source read straight through, alongside Ephesians 6 at 1:1-4 and Psalm 95 at 1:4-27. And the theological work is exact: what makes Enos's guilt swept away is not the content of the promise but the character of the promiser, which is Titus 1:2's entire argument.

1:6.note: 'And I, Enos, knew that God could not lie; wherefore, my guilt was swept away.' The KJV says God cannot lie exactly once, and that verse also contains the phrase Enos gave his father three verses earlier ('concerning eternal life') and the promise-language the chapter runs on. Enos shifts the modal from present to past to fit the narrative — 'cannot' to 'could not' — which is the ordinary adjustment a borrowing makes and not an argument against it. The inference in 'wherefore' is Titus's: because the promiser cannot lie, the promise is as good as performed.

1:8.text: And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.

provenance.other: “thy faith hath made thee whole” occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Matthew 9:22, Mark 5:34, Mark 10:52, Luke 8:48, Luke 17:19). Mark 5:34 and Luke 8:48 are the only two that also carry a dismissal ('go in peace'), which is what Enos's 'go to it' — 1920 'go to' — reproduces.
provenance.alternative: With five KJV homes the formula cannot be pinned to one verse; Matthew 9 is an equally good candidate, since it holds 'thy sins be forgiven thee' (9:2) and 'thy faith hath made thee whole' (9:22) in a single chapter, as Enos 1:5-8 does.
provenance.significance: The dismissal formula belongs to physical healing in every one of its five KJV homes — a haemorrhage, a blindness, a leprosy. Enos is not healed of anything; he is forgiven. The transfer is the finding: the Gospels' word for a body restored is applied to a conscience, and the surrounding verse supplies the reason it can be — the faith is 'in Christ, whom thou hast not heard nor seen', so the formula that in Mark requires touching the hem is here made to work at a distance of six hundred years. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the sentence means more if the reader remembers what it normally cures.

1:8.note: 'Because of thy faith in Christ, whom thou hast not heard nor seen … go to it, thy faith hath made thee whole.' A healing dismissal used as an absolution. 1830's 'go to it' is a compositorial mangling of the KJV's 'go thy way' / 'go in peace' that 1920 tidied to 'go to'; the underlying gesture is the Gospel dismissal in either edition. Note also that 1830 reads 'whom thou hast not heard nor seen' where 1920 reads 'never before heard nor seen' — the first edition's flat negative is the harder and more Johannine reading (compare 1 Peter 1:8, 'whom having not seen, ye love').

1:8.text: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

provenance.other: “manifest in the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:16.
provenance.alternative: 'Manifest in the flesh' may have reached the text through the ordinary theological English of 1829 rather than directly from 1 Timothy; the phrase was creedal currency.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 3:16 is the KJV's compact creed — 'God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels' — and Enos's voice uses its central clause to date an event that has not happened yet. The whole difficulty the verse creates for the Book of Mormon's chronology is concentrated in this borrowing: the phrase for the incarnation is taken from a letter written after it, and used to promise it. That is what CONVENTIONS §3a means by treating failed availability as the finding rather than the filter.

1:8.note: 'And many years passeth away, before that he shall manifest himself in the flesh.' The KJV's one occurrence of the phrase is 1 Timothy 3:16, and the Book of Mormon converts it from passive to reflexive — 'was manifest' becomes 'shall manifest himself' — which is the change a prophecy has to make to a creed. 1830's 'passeth' (1920 'pass') keeps the KJV's habit of a present-tense verb in a future clause.

1:9.text: And Hannah answered and said, No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD.

provenance.other: “poured out my soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 1:15. Psalm 42:4 has 'I pour out my soul in me' in the present tense and without the completed sense Enos needs.
provenance.significance: Hannah's line is a defence against a charge of drunkenness: Eli watched her lips move without sound and assumed she was drunk, and she answered that she had 'poured out my soul before the LORD'. It is the KJV's definitive statement that inaudible, bodily, unseemly-looking prayer is real prayer — which is exactly the apologia Enos 1:2-9 is making for a day-and-night wrestle in a forest. Hannah's prayer is also a prayer for a son who is then given to the Lord, and Enos's is a prayer for a people and then for a record; both are answered by a promise rather than by an immediate gift.

1:9.note: 'I did pour out my whole soul unto God for them.' The one KJV verse with the phrase is Hannah's, and the Book of Mormon's only addition is the intensifier 'whole'. The substitution of 'unto God' for 'before the LORD' is worth noting because it is the same preposition Enos used of the wrestle at 1:2 — the chapter consistently prefers 'before' and 'unto' where the KJV has the other. Hannah is the right model for a chapter about a prayer that looks like a struggle and is heard as a vow.

1:10.text: But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will recompense their way upon their own heads, saith the Lord GOD.

provenance.other: “upon their own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 11:21. The related formulations are singular — 'upon his own head' (1 Kings 2:32-33, Esther 9:25) or 'upon thine own head' (Obadiah 15) — and only Ezekiel has the plural possessive Enos uses.
provenance.alternative: 'Upon their own heads' is idiomatic retribution-language and may have reached the text through general biblical English rather than from Ezekiel specifically.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 11 is the chapter in which the glory of the LORD leaves Jerusalem, and 11:16-20 is the promise to the scattered — 'yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come … and I will give them one heart' — immediately qualified in 11:21 by the recompense on those whose heart walks after abominations. Enos 1:10 is that pair of sentences compressed: a land given and not cursed, and transgressions brought down on the transgressors' own heads. The Book of Mormon's whole diaspora premise is Ezekiel 11:16's, and the verse it quotes is the one that limits the promise.

1:10.note: 'Their transgressions will I bring down with sorrow upon their own heads.' The retribution clause is Ezekiel's singleton; the verb that governs it is not. 'Bring down … with sorrow' is Jacob's, spoken three times in Genesis about losing his sons — 'ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave' — and this is a promise about the sons of a Jacob, spoken to his grandson. If the compound is deliberate it is a fine piece of work: the sorrow the patriarch feared for himself is transferred to the heads of the descendants who caused it.

1:12.text: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.

provenance.other: “with all diligence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 4:23 ('Keep thy heart with all diligence'). The KJV's other diligence formulas are 'with diligence' (Romans 12:8) and 'all diligence' (2 Peter 1:5).
provenance.alternative: 'With all diligence' had become an ordinary English collocation by 1829 and may not be reaching for Proverbs at all.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 4 is the KJV's set-piece of a father instructing a son — 'Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father' (4:1) — and it is the passage Enos 1:1-3 has already been describing without quoting: words often heard from a father, to be kept and not let depart, which 'sunk deep into my heart' against Proverbs 4:21's 'keep them in the midst of thine heart'. When the phrase 'with all diligence' finally surfaces at 1:12 it comes from the next verse of the same passage. The chapter's opening claim about paternal teaching and its central act of persevering prayer are drawn from one column of Proverbs.

1:12.note: 'After I had prayed, and labored with all diligence, the Lord said unto me, I will grant unto thee according to thy desires.' A KJV singleton, and one whose home verse concerns the keeping of a heart — which is what the chapter has been doing since 1:3. The granting formula in the same sentence is Psalm 20:4's, the one KJV verse with 'grant thee according to' ('Grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfil all thy counsel'), so the verse holds two singletons and both of them are about the desires of a heart.

1:13.text: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

provenance.other: “holy arm” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 98:1 and Isaiah 52:10. Psalm 98:1's arm 'hath gotten him the victory'; Isaiah 52:10's is bared before the nations so that they may see salvation, which is the sense Enos needs.
provenance.significance: Enos asks that a record be preserved 'by the power of his holy arm' so that it 'might be brought forth, at some future day, unto the Lamanites, that perhaps they might be brought unto salvation'. Isaiah 52:10 is the one verse in which the holy arm is made bare for exactly that purpose: 'in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God'. The prayer is Isaiah 52:10 turned into a petition — a bared arm, a watching gentile audience, and salvation seen at the far end of the earth. The Book of Mormon's account of its own coming forth is written in the vocabulary of the servant songs, which is where 1 Nephi 21-22 also goes.

1:13.note: 'That the Lord God would preserve a record of my people … even if it so be, by the power of his holy arm, that it might be brought forth, at some future day, unto the Lamanites, that perhaps they might be brought unto salvation.' Two verses in the KJV have a holy arm and only one has it made bare so that a distant people may see salvation. The choice between them is decided by everything around the phrase, not by the phrase itself, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation.

1:15.text: And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.

provenance.other: “whatsoever ye shall ask” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Matthew 21:22, John 14:13, John 15:16, John 16:23); only Matthew 21:22 has 'believing, ye shall receive'. “ask in faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:6.
provenance.significance: Matthew 21:22 is the promise attached to the withered fig tree and the moving of the mountain — a saying about faith that removes an obstacle, given in the temple week. Enos applies it to the survival of a text across centuries, which is a mountain of a different kind, and then reports at 1:16-17 that the promise was converted into a covenant. The addition Enos makes to Matthew is James's: 'ask in faith' is James 1:6's, a KJV singleton, and its continuation 'nothing wavering' explains Enos 1:11's otherwise odd boast that his faith 'began to be unshaken'.

1:15.note: 'Whatsoever thing ye shall ask in faith, believing that ye shall receive in the name of Christ, ye shall receive it.' A composite of the two New Testament sayings about asking: Matthew 21:22's clause supplies the frame and its exact 'believing, ye shall receive', James 1:6 supplies 'ask in faith', and the Johannine 'in my name' is normalized to 'in the name of Christ'. The Book of Mormon presents this as something the Lord 'had said unto me', so the chapter is quoting its own prior revelation — but the words it quotes are three New Testament verses fused.

1:16.text: But hath in due times manifested his word through preaching, which is committed unto me according to the commandment of God our Saviour;

provenance.other: “due time” occurs in exactly six KJV verses (Deuteronomy 32:35, Romans 5:6, 1 Corinthians 15:8, 1 Timothy 2:6, Titus 1:3, 1 Peter 5:6), so the phrase is not rare. Titus 1:3 is preferred here only because Titus 1:2 stands behind Enos 1:6 and 1:3.
provenance.alternative: 'In his own due time' is unremarkable English and may owe nothing to any particular verse; the link is carried entirely by the Titus 1:2 borrowing at 1:6.
provenance.significance: Titus 1:3 is the verse in which a promise made 'before the world began' is discharged: God 'hath in due times manifested his word through preaching'. Enos's covenant is that the record will be brought forth to the Lamanites 'in his own due time' — the same deferral, applied to a text rather than to a gospel, and the same word for it. Read with the link at 1:6, the whole promise-and-fulfilment structure of the chapter's second half is Titus 1:2-3's two verses stretched across fifteen.

1:16.note: 'He covenanted with me that he would bring them forth unto the Lamanites, in his own due time.' On its own this would be common vocabulary and would belong in the exclusion register. It is catalogued because the previous verse of Titus is a demonstrable source for Enos 1:6 — 'cannot lie' being a KJV singleton — and because the two Titus verses account, in their own order, for eternal life at 1:3, God's truthfulness at 1:6, due time here, and preaching at 1:26.

1:17.text: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11, possibly via Hebrews 3:11 / 4:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “into my rest” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Psalm 95:11, Hebrews 3:11, Hebrews 4:3 and Hebrews 4:5 — one psalm and its three New Testament citations. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence: Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11 differ at 'Unto whom'/'So', 'that'/nothing and 'should'/'shall', and Enos reproduces none of those points, so the verse cannot settle its own mediation.
provenance.alternative: 'My soul did rest' shares one content word with the source and could be independent devotional idiom; the case rests on the sequence begun at 1:4, not on this clause.
provenance.significance: The third stop on the Psalm 95 run begun at 1:4. Psalm 95:11 is the psalm's terminal threat — the generation that would not hear the voice does not enter God's rest — and Hebrews 3-4 turns it into the New Testament's central argument that faith is what enters rest ('we which have believed do enter into rest', 4:3). Enos 1:12-17 is that argument narrated: he prays, the Lord grants 'because of thy faith', a covenant is made, and 'my soul did rest'. What the psalm denies to unbelief the chapter grants to belief, which is Hebrews' reading and not the psalm's.

1:17.note: 'I knew it would be according to the covenant which he had made; wherefore, my soul did rest.' Verbal contact is thin — one word — and the link is proposed on the strength of the chapter's demonstrated march down Psalm 95: the maker of 95:6 at 1:4, the voice of 95:7 at 1:5, the rest of 95:11 here, and 'the place of my rest' at 1:27. Hardy attaches Psalm 95:11 to Enos 1:4; the wording that answers it is at this verse and at 1:27, which is why the exclusion register carries an entry at 1:4 explaining the relocation.

1:19.text: And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things.

provenance.other: “heard and seen” in that order occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 2:20 and Revelation 22:8; the far commoner KJV order is 'seen and heard' (Luke 7:22, John 3:32, Acts 4:20, Acts 22:15, 1 John 1:3). Enos has the rarer order.
provenance.alternative: The pairing of hearing and seeing is a stock witness formula and the order may be accidental.
provenance.significance: Revelation 22:8 is a book's closing self-attestation — 'And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen' — placed exactly where Enos places his, eight verses from the end of his own record. Both are first-person signatures by a named writer vouching for what he personally received, and both are followed by a vision of the end (Revelation 22:12-14; Enos 1:27). The position in the book, not the phrase, is what makes the echo interesting.

1:19.note: 'Testifying of the things which I had heard and seen.' Enos has already used the pair negatively at 1:8, where Christ is the one 'whom thou hast not heard nor seen'; here the same two verbs are affirmed of the prophet's own experience. That the order is the rare one, and that the KJV verse carrying it is a writer signing off his book, is what raises this above the common witness formula.

1:20.text: And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents.

provenance.route: Genesis 25:27 and Genesis 27:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “dwelling in tents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 25:27, and “cunning hunter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “quiver and thy bow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 27:3, and “hairy garment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 25:25.
provenance.significance: Enos's ethnography of the Lamanites is assembled out of the KJV's Esau. Two of its clauses are singletons from the Jacob-and-Esau narrative — 'dwelling in tents' from Genesis 25:27 and the bow from Genesis 27:3's 'thy quiver and thy bow' — and the description around them (a skin girded about the loins, raw meat, wandering in the wilderness) is the KJV's portrait of the hairy hunter who 'came out red, all over like an hairy garment' (25:25). The metalepsis is severe and worth stating plainly: Genesis 25:27 assigns tent-dwelling to JACOB and hunting to ESAU, and Enos gives both to the brother-people while his own hunt at 1:3 puts him in Esau's role. The verse that supplies the vocabulary for othering the Lamanites is the verse that says the two brothers were twins.

1:20.note: 'Feading upon beasts of prey, dwelling in tents, and wandering about in the wilderness, with a short skin girded about their loins … and their skill was in the bow.' Three KJV singletons from two adjacent chapters of Genesis, all from the Esau material, gathered into one sentence of description. The 1830 spellings ('feading', 'girded' where 1920 reads 'girdle') are compositorial and do not bear on the judgment. What does bear on it is that Enos, son of Jacob, is describing his kinsmen in the words the KJV uses for Jacob's twin — and that the exclusion register carries the rival proposal, Elijah's leather girdle at 2 Kings 1:8, which fits the clothing but not the genealogy.

1:22.text: And he said, If now I have found grace in thy sight, O LORD, let my LORD, I pray thee, go among us; for it is a stiffnecked people; and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for thine inheritance.

provenance.other: “stiffnecked people” occurs in exactly six KJV verses (Exodus 32:9, 33:3, 33:5, 34:9, Deuteronomy 9:6, 9:13), so the phrase alone identifies nothing; Exodus 34:9 is chosen because of what 1:23 does with 2 Corinthians 3. 1830 hyphenates 'stiff-necked'; the KJV and 1920 do not.
provenance.alternative: Any of the six KJV verses would supply the phrase, and Deuteronomy 9:6 is the one a reader of the Pentateuch would meet in a prophetic-rebuke setting.
provenance.significance: 'Stiffnecked people' is the golden-calf verdict, and Exodus 34 is where Moses pleads it as a reason for pardon rather than for destruction — 'for it is a stiffnecked people; and pardon our iniquity'. It is also the chapter of the veil (34:33-35). That matters because Enos's very next verse borrows 2 Corinthians 3:12's 'great plainness of speech', and 2 Corinthians 3 is Paul's argument built precisely on Exodus 34's veil: unveiled boldness against Moses' covered face and Israel's blinded mind. Enos 1:22-23 pairs the stiffnecked people of Exodus 34 with the unveiled plainness that 2 Corinthians 3 sets against them, which is a coherent reading of the two passages together and not a coincidence of two stock phrases.

1:22.note: 'And the people were a stiff-necked people, hard to understand.' The epithet is common enough to be excluded on its own terms; it is catalogued because of its neighbour. Exodus 34 gives both halves of what Enos 1:22-23 needs — a stiffnecked people and a veil — and 2 Corinthians 3:12-14, the source of 1:23's KJV singleton, is a sustained reading of that chapter. The pair is the argument; neither verse would carry it alone.

1:23.text: Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech:

provenance.other: “great plainness of speech” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:12. The phrase renders parrhesia, which the KJV elsewhere gives as 'boldness'; the 'plainness' rendering is peculiar to this verse.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence continues: 'And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face … but their minds were blinded' (3:13-14). Plainness of speech is defined in its home verse against Moses' veil and against a hardened Israel — which is exactly the audience Enos has just named at 1:22, 'a stiff-necked people', the golden-calf epithet from the same Exodus chapter that gives Paul his veil. Recover the context and Enos's preaching method turns out to be argued from scripture: to a people in the condition of Exodus 34, the apostolic answer is the unveiled face of 2 Corinthians 3. Compare Hays on metalepsis; the suppressed term here is the veil, which Enos never mentions and which supplies his whole rationale.

1:23.note: 'There was nothing short of these things, and exceeding great plainness of speech, would keep them from going down speedily to destruction.' A four-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly, with 'exceeding' added in the Book of Mormon's own intensifying idiom. What makes the link more than a phrase-match is that its source verse and its neighbour verse in Enos are drawing on the same chapter of Exodus from two directions — Exodus 34's stiffnecked people at 1:22 and Exodus 34's veil, via Paul, here.

1:27.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “put on immortality” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 15:53 and 15:54; the phrase appears nowhere else in the Bible. “rejoice in the day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:16.
provenance.significance: The clause is the hinge of Paul's resurrection chapter, and Enos takes it with its own tense distinction intact: 15:53 has 'must put on' and 15:54 'shall have put on', and Enos writes 'shall put on', the future the day requires. The framing verb is Philippians 2:16's — 'that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain' — a KJV singleton whose context is a minister wondering whether his labour was wasted, which is the anxiety Enos has been carrying since 1:14 ('our struggles were vain') and 1:20 ('our labors were vain'). The book's last sentence answers its own repeated word.

1:27.note: 'I rejoice in the day when my mortal shall put on immortality.' Two New Testament phrases, one of them confined to a single pair of verses in the whole Bible, fused into a clause of eleven words. It sits below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the rarity, per CONVENTIONS §2. Note that Enos says 'my mortal' where Paul says 'this mortal' — the possessive is the Book of Mormon's, and it is what turns a doctrinal statement into a deathbed one.

1:27.text: In my Father’s house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.

provenance.route: John 14:2-3 with Matthew 25:34 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “mansions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:2. “prepare a place for you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 14:2 and 14:3. “ye blessed of my Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34, as does “prepared for you from the foundation”.
provenance.significance: The last sentence of the book of Enos is two of the most familiar consolations in the KJV welded together at the seam where they share a word. John 14:2-3 promises 'many mansions' and 'I go to prepare a place for you'; Matthew 25:34 has the King say 'Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world'. Both have a place prepared and one has the summons; Enos writes 'Come unto me ye blessed, there is a place prepared for you in the mansions of my Father'. Recover the contexts and the two are not compatible in the ordinary way: John's is spoken to friends before a death, Matthew's is spoken at a judgment that divides sheep from goats — and Enos, who has spent the chapter praying for a people he expects to be destroyed, ends by hearing the sheep-side of the judgment in the language of the upper room.

1:27.note: 'He will say unto me, Come unto me ye blessed, there is a place prepared for you in the mansions of my Father.' The word 'mansions' appears once in the entire King James Bible and Enos has it, in the plural, attached to 'my Father' exactly as John 14:2 attaches it to 'my Father's house'. The summons is Matthew 25:34's, altered from 'Come, ye blessed of my Father' to 'Come unto me ye blessed' — which imports the invitation of Matthew 11:28 into the judgment scene and is the small change that makes the sentence Enos's rather than Matthew's.

1:27.text: He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness.

provenance.other: “see his face with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 33:26; Enos substitutes 'pleasure' for 'joy'. No other KJV verse promises the sight of God's face as the outcome of prayer.
provenance.alternative: A single altered word could mean the phrase came from memory rather than from the page, or that a common devotional idiom underlies both.
provenance.significance: Elihu's speech is the closest thing in the KJV to a summary of the book of Enos: a man is spared from 'going down to the pit' because a ransom is found (33:24), 'he shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness' (33:26). Enos 1:26-27 runs the same three beats in the same order — 'I must soon go down to my grave', the prayers of the whole chapter, and then 'I see his face'. The one word Enos changes is the last: Job's 'joy' becomes 'pleasure'. And the face he expects to see closes the Genesis 32 frame opened at 1:2, where Jacob's wrestle ended with 'I have seen God face to face'.

1:27.note: 'Then shall I see his face with pleasure.' Four of the five words are Job 33:26's and the KJV has them nowhere else. The substitution is the interesting part: 'joy' in Job describes the restored man's own gladness, and 'pleasure' shifts the register toward the pleasure of the seeing, which is the direction Enos's whole closing sentence moves — from being forgiven to being welcomed. Read with 1:26's 'I must soon go down to my grave' against Job 33:24's 'going down to the pit', the last two verses of the book work through Elihu's paragraph in order.

1:27.text: Thus saith the LORD, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?

provenance.route: Isaiah 66:1 or Acts 7:49 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the place of my rest” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 66:1 and Acts 7:49. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence: the two differ at 'where is the'/'what', 'that'/'will' and the address formula, and Enos reproduces none of those points, so mediation cannot be settled from this verse and is recorded as uncertain.
provenance.significance: In the KJV 'the place of my rest' is God's own phrase for the temple he does not need — 'the heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool … where is the house that ye build unto me?' — and it occurs twice, in Isaiah and in Stephen's speech quoting Isaiah. Enos takes a phrase God uses to refuse a building and applies it to his own death: the place of God's rest becomes the place of Enos's, 'which is with my redeemer'. That reversal is the finding, and it completes the Psalm 95 thread begun at 1:4, where the rest was something a generation was sworn out of.

1:27.note: 'And I soon go to the place of my rest, which is with my redeemer; for I know that in him I shall rest.' The phrase is confined to one Old Testament verse and its one New Testament quotation, and Enos has it exactly. Which of the two he has cannot be determined — the mediation check finds no point of divergence inside the borrowed words — and the catalogue records that rather than guessing. Stephen's version has the mild attraction of context, since Acts 7 is a martyr's last speech reciting the fathers, which is the genre of Enos 1:25-27.
